title: Nora Fatehi Walked Out in Red and Stopped Toronto Cold. The First Indian Woman to Headline a World Cup Opening Just Did It in Canada.
excerpt: Hundreds of dancers, an official anthem inspired by a Moroccan football chant, and 20 million YouTube views in a day — Nora Fatehi turned BMO Field into a Bollywood stage, and the diaspora was front row.
body:
The pitch at BMO Field was a sea of red and gold, the Canadian flag stitched into the grass like a stage set, when Alessia Cara handed the night over. And then she arrived — **Nora Fatehi**, in a red ensemble that caught every floodlight in Toronto, flanked by hundreds of dancers, and for the next few minutes the second opening ceremony of the 2026 FIFA World Cup belonged entirely to her.

This is the kind of moment Indian entertainment has spent two decades waiting for. Not a cameo. Not a Bollywood star politely waving from a VIP box. A headline slot, on football's biggest stage, in front of a global broadcast audience — and the woman holding it was the *Saki Saki* girl who once danced in the background of other people's songs.

The occasion was the Toronto leg of the World Cup's twin opening ceremonies, staged Friday ahead of co-hosts Canada's tournament opener against Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mexico City had gone first on Thursday, with **Shakira** and **Burna Boy** delivering the marquee anthem. Toronto answered with its own glittering lineup — **Alanis Morissette**, **Alessia Cara**, **Michael Bublé**, **Jessie Reyez**, Palestinian breakout **Elyanna**, French star **Vegedream**, and Canadian artists **William Prince** and producer **Sanjoy**. And nestled in that roster of Grammy winners and global names was a Bollywood performer holding her own.

> "It's been so exciting to be a part of such a massive mainstream lineup! I perform at the opening ceremony in Toronto while Shakira and Burna Boy do the opening ceremony in Mexico. I've worked all my life to reach this level, to be sharing opportunities with such icons!" — Nora Fatehi, to Hindustan Times

The night opened with a tribute to Canada's Indigenous peoples, a symbolic journey across the country before the stars hit the stage. Then came Nora, performing **Siir Siir**, one of the official songs of the 2026 World Cup, alongside Vegedream and Sanjoy. The crowd, primed and waiting, erupted. She didn't just sing it — she danced it, the way only she does, the choreography sharp and the vocals electric, the whole spectacle backed by a small army of dancers.

What makes *Siir Siir* fascinating is where it came from. The track isn't a label-manufactured anthem dropped onto an artist. It was Nora's own idea, born in a stadium in Morocco.

> "When I was attending the AFCON matches in Morocco in January, I heard almost 70,000 fans chant 'Siir Siir' in the stadium during every game, and I was in awe. The energy inspired me to reach out to producer Sanjoy and ask him to create a World Cup anthem using this chant." — Nora Fatehi

That instinct paid off in numbers that would make any label blush. Her FIFA track reportedly racked up roughly **20 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours** — outpacing the opening-day haul of Shakira's official anthem *Dai Dai*, which drew 8.2 million in the same window. For an artist who entered the music world only a handful of years ago, sitting atop a first-day chart that includes Shakira is not a footnote. It's a statement.

For the diaspora, the symbolism lands even harder because of *where* this happened. Canada is home to one of the largest, most visible Indian communities outside India — Brampton, Surrey, Scarborough, the whole sprawling Greater Toronto belt. To watch a brown woman command BMO Field, in *their* city, performing for the world while the maple leaf glowed behind her, was the kind of representation that doesn't need a hashtag to explain itself. It just felt like a door opening.

There were grumbles, to be fair — some fans found the broader ceremony underwhelming, and parts of the stadium showed empty seats. But none of that touched Nora's segment, which trended across social media within hours and gave Indian fans, from Toronto to Tooting to Jersey City, a genuine reason to cheer before a single ball was kicked.

Nora Fatehi has spent her career being underestimated — the item-song dancer, the reality-show judge, the glamour act. This was the night the world had to file her under something else entirely: headliner. And she walked out in red and made sure no one would forget it.
